key_facts: placeholder
argument: Modeled P&L for 2 financed skis (~$30k at ~9%/72-84mo = ~$6.5k/yr debt service; commercial rental insurance ~$3.5-5k/yr low end; maintenance/fuel/winterization/registration ~$2.5-3.5k/yr; effective ~$300/day per ski): PESSIMISTIC (10 rental days/ski): ~$6k revenue vs ~$13k costs = -$7k/yr cash loss funded from reduced 401k contributions. BASE (25 days/ski): ~$15k revenue vs ~$13.5k costs = roughly breakeven BEFORE damage incidents, no-shows, platform fees (GetMyBoat takes a cut), self-employment tax, and dozens of weekends of the user's labor. OPTIMISTIC (45 days/ski, top-decile for a side-hustler): ~$27k revenue, ~$12k pre-tax profit — but this requires near-every-summer-weekend availability alongside a W-2 job AND the existing Lake Salt Mobile Bar, whose peak season is the same summer weekends. The friend's 15-month payoff implies ~$2k/mo net, i.e. 55-70+ rental days per ski per season with near-zero customer-acquisition cost and informal trust-based handoffs (likely no commercial insurance drag) inside a tight community. That is the causal engine of her result and it does not replicate via FB Marketplace listings in a market with established competitors. The financing structure makes it worse: funding payments by cutting 401k contributions means the pessimistic/base scenarios are paid for with lost tax-advantaged compound growth on a rapidly depreciating, liability-heavy asset. The 'own it free and clear' end-state is owning a 3-year-old high-hour rental PWC worth ~half its price. If the itch persists, the capital-light test is renting out ONE used cash-purchased ski, or partnering skis into existing Lake Salt event clientele — not two financed new units.
biggest_risk: Biggest risk to this analysis: the user may live in a high-demand tourist waterfront market where day rates and utilization run well above inland norms, and could cross-sell to Lake Salt's event clientele — pushing the base case toward the optimistic one. Biggest risk if they build anyway: an uninsured or under-insured renter injury (specialty rental coverage is unavailable in several states and pricey everywhere), turning a marginal side hustle into a five-to-six-figure liability while retirement savings are already reduced.

key_facts: USCG 2024 data: PWCs accounted for ~19% of all reported boating incidents despite being a small share of vessels; PWCs are the only vessel class where blunt-force trauma, not drowning, is the leading cause of death; operator inexperience (436 incidents) is a top-3 contributing factor — exactly the profile of a rental customer (uscgboating.org Recreational Boating Statistics 2024).

Personal PWC insurance policies explicitly exclude and deny claims for commercial/rental use. Renting to strangers on a personal Progressive-type policy (~$100-500/yr) means effectively ZERO coverage the moment money changes hands (Global Marine, Progressive, insuranks.com).

Real commercial livery insurance runs roughly $1,500-$3,500+ per jet ski per year, or ~$5,000-$12,000/yr for a 1-3 ski fleet (specialty carriers like Prime, XINSURANCE; rentrax.com, ownersoasis.com). On 2 skis that alone can exceed the entire hoped-for loan payment coverage from rental income.

Many states regulate PWC rental as a 'livery.' Florida example: livery permit required (operating without one is a first-degree misdemeanor, $1,000 fine), commercial re-registration, and MANDATORY insurance of $500k per person / $1M per event, plus safety-instruction requirements (Fla. Stat. 327.54). FWC has actually charged individuals running informal FB-Marketplace-style jet ski rentals (survivalworld.com news reports).

Waivers help but are not a shield: courts void them for gross negligence, statutory violations (e.g., unlicensed livery), or negligent entrustment (renting to intoxicated, underage, or clearly inexperienced users). The rental company in In re Luxury Jet Ski Rentals won only because it was licensed, documented, and had enforceable signed waivers — the informal FB model has none of that.

If an uninsured informal rental injures or kills someone, the owner is personally liable: judgment can reach wages, savings, and home equity (homestead protection varies by state); an LLC formed without insurance is easily pierced or simply holds the asset while the plaintiff sues the owner-operator personally for their own negligence. The user's W-2 wages and house are directly exposed.

The coworker's 15-month payoff almost certainly worked because it was uninsured/unpermitted and nothing went wrong — survivorship bias, not a risk model. One trauma injury (median jet ski injury verdicts/settlements routinely reach six-seven figures) wipes out years of profit and more.
argument: From a liability and regulatory lens this plan, as described, is uninsurable-by-default and personally ruinous in the tail case. The economics the user is copying — friend paid off skis in 15 months via FB Marketplace — only pencil out because that operation skipped commercial insurance ($1.5k-$3.5k per ski/yr) and, likely, livery permitting. Do it legally and the fixed costs (commercial livery policy, permit, commercial registration, LLC, safety compliance) consume most or all of the margin on a 1-2 ski seasonal operation; do it the friend's way and every rental hour bets the user's home, savings, and future wages against the single worst injury profile in recreational boating — machines that kill by blunt-force trauma, handed to inexperienced strangers, with a personal policy that denies the claim outright the moment it learns money changed hands. A waiver scrawled via Facebook Messenger will not survive a suit premised on unlicensed livery operation and negligent entrustment. And this user is uniquely poorly positioned to absorb the tail risk: they are funding loan payments out of retirement contributions, meaning there is no cash buffer, and they already own another attachable business (Lake Salt Mobile Bar) and W-2 income stream. If they insist on jet ski exposure, the modified path is to list through a platform with built-in commercial coverage (GetMyBoat/Boatsetter-style, ideally captained/accompanied rentals) after confirming their state's livery rules — but the FB-Marketplace informal model should be treated as disqualified, not merely risky.
biggest_risk: A single serious renter injury or death (the modal PWC casualty is blunt-force trauma to an inexperienced operator) while operating as an uninsured, unpermitted livery: the personal PWC policy denies the claim, the waiver is voided for statutory violation/negligent entrustment, and a six-to-seven-figure judgment attaches to the user's wages, savings, and home — turning a retirement-contribution-funded side hustle into personal financial destruction.

key_facts: Funding source is retirement: skis 2026 run ~$8k-$20k each; 2 skis + trailer financed ~$28k-$38k at 6-12% APR (powersports rates by credit tier per LendingTree/finder 2026) => ~$600-$750/mo over 60 months.

Because 401k deferrals are pre-tax, freeing ~$700/mo after-tax requires cutting ~$850-$950/mo of contributions; if that drops the user below the employer match threshold, the loss is larger — skipping a typical 3% match alone compounds to ~$266k over 35 years at 7% (24/7 Wall St / Fidelity 2026 analyses).
Even without match loss, ~$900/mo diverted for 5 years at ~7% real return is ~$64k at payoff, growing to roughly $350k-$490k by a retirement 25-30 years out — that is the true price of the skis.

Jet skis depreciate ~20-22% in year 1 and ~8%/yr after; rental units with high engine hours fare worse. Two skis bought for ~$30k are plausibly worth $10k-$14k free-and-clear after 5 years — the celebrated 'paid-off asset' is a wasting asset.

Commercial/rental insurance is the hidden killer: personal PWC policies exclude commercial rental; rental liability coverage runs ~$3k-$7k per ski per year, and GetMyBoat offers no PWC insurance (marina policies often require 5+ units). Add $1.5k-$3k/yr per ski maintenance, storage, winterization, fuel — plus seasonality (3-5 rentable months in most non-Sun-Belt lake markets).
argument: Strip away the story and this trade is: sell ~$55k-$65k of pre-tax retirement contributions (worth $350k-$490k at retirement via compounding, and dramatically more if any employer match is forfeited) to acquire an asset worth maybe $10k-$14k at payoff, plus whatever net rental cash flow survives insurance, maintenance, storage, platform fees, and seasonality. The coworker's 15-month payoff was driven by a zero-cost distribution channel (a tight community network) the user explicitly lacks, and likely by running uninsured or under-insured — proper commercial PWC liability at $3k-$7k/ski/yr can consume most of a small operator's gross in a market with existing competitors and a short season. 'Paid-off asset at the end' is an ownership-bias illusion: paid-off does not mean valuable, and a depreciating, liability-generating machine is close to the worst asset class to buy with retirement dollars. The dominant alternative is nearly free: Lake Salt Mobile Bar already has brand, equipment, insurance, and booking flow — one extra event per month likely nets more than two rented jet skis, with zero new debt, zero new liability exposure, and no raid on the 401k. If the user still wants watersports exposure, the capital-light version is partnering with or cross-promoting an existing local operator to Lake Salt's event clients.
biggest_risk: Biggest risk of my recommendation being wrong: if the user is in a year-round Sun-Belt market, keeps full employer match, and genuinely achieves the coworker's utilization, net cash flow could beat my base case — but even then a single uninsured renter injury (personal policies exclude commercial use) could wipe out years of gains, so the downside asymmetry stands.

key_facts: placeholder
argument: Operationally this is a second summer-weekend service business stacked on top of an existing one. Each rental is not passive: P2P owners trailer, launch, retrieve, fuel, clean, brief renters, and inspect for damage — call it 2-4 hours per booking, and bookings cluster on the exact Saturdays Lake Salt Mobile Bar is pouring at events. The user cannot be at a boat ramp at 9am and 5pm while also running a bar gig; hiring help kills margin. Distribution is worse than assumed: FB Marketplace bans rental/service listings, so the coworker's playbook was really her community network — which the user admits they don't have. The insured-platform fallback is thin: Boatsetter's policy excludes PWCs entirely, and GetMyBoat requires the owner to bring their own commercial liability coverage, a niche, costly policy; renting uninsured through FB Groups puts personal assets at risk in an injury-heavy activity. Add ~15 rentable weekends a year, weather cancellations, no-shows, and damage disputes against 12 months of loan payments funded by raiding retirement contributions, and the operations math says don't build. If the itch persists, the low-risk test is renting a competitor's ski to learn the ramp workflow, or partnering the mobile bar with an existing rental operator for cross-referrals instead of owning depreciating financed assets.
biggest_risk: An uninsured or under-insured renter injury during an off-platform (FB group/word-of-mouth) rental: PWC rental use is excluded from personal policies and from Boatsetter's program, so one accident could produce a liability judgment that dwarfs the skis' value and reaches the user's personal assets — while they're still making loan payments out of reduced 401k contributions.

key_facts: Peer rental rates are strong: inland US jet ski rentals commonly run $55-100/hr and ~$199-300/day (Mesa AZ: ~$199 for 2 hrs); two skis rented 2 full weekend days at ~$250/day each gross ~$4,000/month in season (getmyboat.com, rentrax.com, 2025-26).

Entry cost is modest: used Sea-Doos start around $4,000 (avg ~$9,500 used); new Rec-Lite models from $6,999-8,499; dealer financing as low as 3.99% APR/36mo WAC — a single used ski + trailer can be under $10k financed, with payments in the low hundreds/month (pwctrader.com, jetdrift.com).

Platforms de-risk liability and demand generation: GetMyBoat and Boatsetter list private PWCs, handle bookings/payments, and Boatsetter offers commercial rental coverage (20-35% commission with their insurance, 10% if owner carries own); standalone PWC rental insurance is obtainable ($500-$3,000+/yr small scale via Prime, XINSURANCE, Global Marine).

Demand is growing, not fading: PWC market projected ~6% CAGR through 2035, with rental/marine tourism specifically expanding; summer concentration means 60%+ of revenue lands in a few peak months — and the user is entering with the 2027 season available to prepare for (futuremarketinsights.com, ibisworld.com).

Depreciation stabilizes after year 3 (30-40% first 3 years, then flattens), so buying a 2-3 year old well-maintained Yamaha/Sea-Doo captures most of the value curve; Yamahas lose only ~23% between years 2 and 5 (jdpower.com).

Real synergy exists: Lake Salt Mobile Bar gives the user a lake-adjacent local audience, event clientele (lake parties, bachelorette/birthday groups who also rent skis), proven local-marketing chops, existing LLC/business infrastructure, and cross-promotion channels the coworker's word-of-mouth-only model lacked.
The coworker's 15-month payoff is a directly comparable local proof point in the same market — same area, same FB Marketplace channel — demonstrating local demand exists despite competitors.
argument: The honest bull case: this is a proven, asset-backed micro-business with a working local comp. The coworker paid off her skis in ~15 months in this same market using only FB Marketplace and word of mouth — that is rare, directly relevant validation that local demand clears the competitor supply. The unit economics genuinely work at small scale: a used 2-3-year-old ski bought at ~$5-9k (past the steep depreciation cliff) rented at $250-300/day needs only ~2-3 booked days per month to cover a financed payment plus insurance, and peak-summer weekends in lake towns routinely book solid. Unlike most side hustles, the downside is bounded by a liquid hard asset — used skis resell readily on the same FB Marketplace, so a failed experiment recovers most of principal. The user also has structural advantages the coworker lacked: an existing lake-oriented business (Lake Salt Mobile Bar) with event clientele who are exactly jet-ski renters (lake parties, bachelorette groups), an established local marketing muscle, business banking/LLC scaffolding to shield liability, and delivery capability (they already haul a mobile bar) enabling a delivery upsell competitors may not offer. Platforms like GetMyBoat/Boatsetter solve the two scariest problems — liability insurance and demand beyond one's personal network — for a commission. BUT the strongest honest case requires modifications: (1) start with ONE used ski (~$6-9k), not two new ones, cutting the financed amount roughly 60-70%; (2) run all rentals through Boatsetter/GetMyBoat or a proper commercial PWC policy — never bare FB-Marketplace handshake rentals, which are uninsured liability bombs; (3) form an LLC and title the ski in it; (4) treat the reduced-401k funding as a hard 12-month test: if the ski isn't covering its own payment by summer's end, sell it (recovering most principal) and restore contributions. Under those modifications, the risk-adjusted case is genuinely good; as originally stated (two financed skis, retirement-funded, FB-only), it is not.
biggest_risk: The financing source: payments come from reduced 401k contributions, so a slow season, an injury lawsuit outside platform coverage, or one uninsured wreck doesn't just lose a side hustle — it compounds into lost tax-advantaged retirement growth (and possibly lost employer match), and seasonality means loan payments continue through 6+ dead winter months when revenue is zero.
